data.name: AboutSeoTitle
data.value: About BasketElo | Global Basketball ELO Rankings

data.name: AboutSeoDescription
data.value: Meet the engineer and lifelong basketball fan behind BasketElo, an independent project ranking NBA, European club, and national teams with transparent data and methods.

data.name: AboutHeroTitle
data.value: I grew up with basketball. Then I tried to rank all of it.

data.name: AboutHeroIntro
data.value: Hi, I’m Sergio. I’m an engineer and a lifelong basketball fan. My first trips to an arena came when I was only a few months old. Years later, I spent high school playing, or at least making a determined attempt.

data.name: AboutHeroElo
data.value: Somewhere along the way, I became fascinated by ELO. I am not a chess player, or even much of a chess fan, but the system itself seemed wonderfully elegant to the engineer in me: give it a stream of results and it can place every player on the same scale.

data.name: AboutBeginningTitle
data.value: One rating. Many leagues. How hard could it be?

data.name: AboutBeginningText1
data.value: Could the same idea work for basketball? I wanted to see if one transparent rating could put teams from different leagues on the same map, using little more than the games they played.

data.name: AboutBeginningText2
data.value: I began with European clubs. Once that worked, adding national teams and the NBA felt like a natural next step. At roughly that point, the small experiment politely stopped being small.

data.name: AboutJourneyTitle
data.value: The formula was the easy part. Naturally.

data.name: AboutJourneyIntro
data.value: The interesting part was everything around it: the data, the identities, and the questions that appeared once the rankings existed. This is where a small experiment quietly becomes a data archaeology project.

data.name: SimpleModelDescription
data.value: The first goal was simply to compare European clubs using a transparent ELO model.

data.name: DataFoughtBackDescription
data.value: Archives disagreed, clubs changed names, competitions changed shape, and source IDs turned out to be suspicious aliases rather than real identities.

data.name: MapGotBiggerDescription
data.value: The NBA and national teams joined the project, along with team histories, game explanations, and tools for testing different models.

data.name: StillAskingQuestionsDescription
data.value: Coverage is improving, assumptions remain visible, and a better source or method can still change what the site thinks it knows.

data.name: AboutMarginsTitle
data.value: Built in the margins, occasionally between everything else.

data.name: AboutMarginsText1
data.value: As an engineer, I like building things. As a father of two small daughters, I rarely have more than 30 minutes at a time, and I also like to leave some room for exercise. AI has allowed me to work on BasketElo without needing to be in front of the computer all the time. Without it, this project probably would not have been possible.

data.name: AboutMarginsText2
data.value: That help does not remove the need for judgment. Provenance, tests, versioned models, and visible warnings still matter. The aim is to show what the ratings use, where the games came from, and where the data still has limits.

data.name: AboutStackTitle
data.value: Built by Codex. Watched over by a basketball fan.

data.name: AboutStackText
data.value: BasketElo is built with Codex on Blazor and .NET, then built and deployed directly to production on an OVH VPS. It is a surprisingly effective way to make a website when your free time arrives in tiny, unpredictable parcels.

data.name: AboutStackDisclaimer
data.value: No single line of code has been human reviewed. Or reviewed at all, really. Codex writes, tests, and deploys it directly to production. This is either impressively efficient or a very elaborate way to create suspense.

data.name: MethodSeoTitle
data.value: How Basketball ELO Ratings Work | BasketElo

data.name: MethodSeoDescription
data.value: Learn how BasketElo calculates basketball team ratings using opponent strength, home-court advantage, score margin, competition weight, and transparent ELO formulas.

data.name: MethodHeroText
data.value: A team starts at 1,500. After every game, its rating moves by an amount shaped by the opponent, the result, home court, and the score margin.

data.name: ChessIdeaTitle
data.value: The chess idea, in three moves.

data.name: ChessIdeaIntro
data.value: ELO does not reward every win equally. It first estimates what should happen, then moves each rating according to how surprising the actual result was.

data.name: ExpectDescription
data.value: The rating gap becomes an expected score. Equal players start at 50–50; a 400-point advantage is worth roughly 91%.

data.name: ScoreDescription
data.value: Chess records 1 for a win, 0.5 for a draw, and 0 for a loss. Basketball uses 1 or 0 because rated games require a winner.

data.name: UpdateDescription
data.value: The new rating is the old rating plus K × (actual − expected). An upset therefore moves more points than a routine win.

data.name: EloFormula
data.value: new rating = old rating + K × (actual − expected)

data.name: ModelsComparisonTitle
data.value: Basic and Adjusted ELO answer slightly different questions.

data.name: BasicEloDescription
data.value: Looks only at who won, who lost, and how strong each team was beforehand. It is the clearest reference model.

data.name: AdjustedEloDescription
data.value: Adds the information in the final score. A convincing win can matter more than a narrow one, within a controlled limit.

data.name: DefaultModelMeaning
data.value: “Default” simply means this is the model shown first in the public rankings.

data.name: ModelHistoriesSeparate
data.value: You can switch models there; their histories remain separate.

data.name: WorkedExampleIntro
data.value: Using the current adjusted model, the calculation starts like this:

data.name: EffectiveGapDescription
data.value: The home team receives a 70-point home-court adjustment.

data.name: WinExpectationDescription
data.value: The classic ELO curve uses 400 as its probability scale. Substituting the 170-point gap produces 0.72683, rounded here to 72.7%.

data.name: BaseUpdateDescription
data.value: If the favourite wins, it gains a modest 5.46 points before the score-margin adjustment.

data.name: LimitsTitle
data.value: A useful signal, not a verdict.

data.name: LimitsText1
data.value: ELO describes what past results support right now. It does not know about injuries, line-ups, travel, motivation, or a tactical change that has not appeared in the results yet.

data.name: LimitsText2
data.value: Every rating is tied to a versioned model, so an improved formula can be tested and rebuilt without silently rewriting an older history.
